## Things That Move {#sec-motion}

Everything so far has been about a single picture. Video adds a third coordinate. A video is a sequence of frames, and we write the brightness at pixel (x, y) in frame t as I(x, y, t). It might seem that time makes everything harder, and in general it does. But it also hands us an extraordinarily cheap source of information. In most scenes almost nothing changes from one frame to the next, so the pixels that *do* change are telling us something. Slide 5 of Lecture notes 2 introduces the idea in three lines ([Lecture notes 2, slide 5](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-cs585-template-matching-ncc-pyramids-Jan30.pdf)), and Lecture notes 3 shows how far it can be pushed, all the way to a room that watches children act out a story ([Lecture notes 3](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-kids-room.pdf)).

### Reading video {#sec-reading-video}

OpenCV reads video files and webcams with the same object. Each call to `read` returns a flag that says whether it worked and the next frame as an ordinary image array.

```{python}
cap = cv2.VideoCapture("clip.avi")    # or cv2.VideoCapture(0) for the first webcam

while True:
    ok, frame = cap.read()             # frame is a BGR image, exactly as in Section 1.1
    if not ok:                         # end of the file, or the camera failed
        break
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    # ... process gray here ...

cap.release()
```

The `if not ok` check plays the same role as the `None` check after `cv2.imread`. Without it, the loop crashes at the end of every video, usually with an error that points somewhere else entirely.

### Frame differencing {#sec-frame-differencing}

The simplest motion detector subtracts the previous frame from the current one,

$$
\text{Diff}(x,y,t) = I(x,y,t) - I(x,y,t-1).
$$

Wherever nothing moved, the two frames agree and Diff is near zero. Wherever something moved, it is not. Slide 5 adds two refinements, both posed as questions. One is to compare frames k apart instead of neighbours, with k = 10 as the example. The other is to take the absolute value. Let us understand both.

**Why the absolute value?** Picture a dark square sliding to the right across a light background. At its front edge, pixels that used to show background now show the square, so they get darker and Diff is negative. At its back edge, the square has uncovered background, so those pixels get brighter and Diff is positive. Both edges are motion, and the sign only tells us which edge is which. Taking |Diff| treats them alike. There is a programming reason too, and we met it in @sec-arithmetic-that-bites. Subtract two `uint8` frames directly and the negative values wrap around. In our test, a front-edge pixel whose true difference was −129 came out as 127, because −129 + 256 = 127. So we always widen the type first.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: read the frames of clip.avi"
#| classes: lc-setup
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. Read every frame of clip.avi as a grey image, and set up
# two consecutive frames: prev is frame 9 and gray is frame 10.
cap = cv2.VideoCapture("clip.avi")
frames = []
while True:
    ok, f = cap.read()
    if not ok:
        break
    frames.append(cv2.cvtColor(f, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY))
cap.release()
prev = frames[9].astype(np.int16)
gray = frames[10]
```

```{python}
cur = gray.astype(np.int16)              # int16 holds -255 ... 255 comfortably
diff = np.abs(cur - prev)                # prev is the previous frame, also int16
prev = cur
```

**Why a gap of k frames?** Here a little geometry helps. Suppose a uniformly coloured object of width w moves v pixels per frame, with v smaller than w. Compare two frames. The object's interior is the same colour in both, so the difference is zero there, even though the object is moving. The difference is nonzero only in two bands, one at the front and one at the back, each exactly v pixels wide. In our test the square moved 3 pixels per frame, and the pixels flagged in one row were columns 37 to 39 and 67 to 69, two bands of width 3. A slow object therefore produces only a thin sliver of motion, which noise can easily swamp. Comparing frames k apart is the same as making the object move kv pixels, so the bands become k times wider. With k = 5 our bands grew to 15 pixels each. The price is lag, since the method now reports where things were k frames ago as well as where they are now.

**How big must a difference be?** The KidsRoom slides define motion as any pixel with Diff > 0 ([Lecture notes 3, slide 16](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-kids-room.pdf)). In a real camera that would mark the whole image as moving, because every pixel carries noise. We can be quantitative about this. Suppose each pixel's value fluctuates from frame to frame with standard deviation σ, independently in each frame. The variance of a difference of two independent quantities is the sum of their variances, so

$$
\operatorname{Var}\big[I(t) - I(t-1)\big] = \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 = 2\sigma^2, \qquad \text{so the noise in Diff has standard deviation } \sqrt{2}\,\sigma .
$$

Subtracting frames makes the noise *worse* by a factor of √2, about 1.41. Our test frames had σ = 3, and the measured standard deviation of the difference in a region with no motion was 4.27, against the predicted 4.24. A threshold of three or four times √2 σ keeps false alarms rare. We used τ = 15, about 3.5 standard deviations, and in a motionless block of 6,400 pixels exactly one was wrongly flagged.

```{python}
tau = 15
moving = (diff > tau).astype(np.uint8)      # 1 where something changed
```

To estimate σ for your own camera, point it at a still scene, take two frames, and compute the standard deviation of their difference. Divide by √2 and you have it.

Write `estimate_sigma(frame_a, frame_b)`, which estimates the per-pixel noise σ from two frames of a still scene with the √2 rule of @sec-frame-differencing. The video was made with σ = 3. The check applies your function to the still strip of frames 9 and 10 and prints the estimate together with the threshold τ = 3.5√2 σ it suggests. Your number will probably come out well below 3, because the clip is stored as Motion JPEG and compression smooths away a good part of the fine noise. That is a useful lesson in itself. The noise we can measure is the noise in the file we have, not the noise that came off the sensor.

    sigma = estimate_sigma(a, b)

### Subtracting the background instead {#sec-subtracting-the-background-instead}

Frame differencing finds the edges of moving things. Often we want the whole thing. The KidsRoom tracked children as *background-difference blobs* ([Lecture notes 3, slide 13](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-kids-room.pdf)), comparing each frame not with the previous frame but with a picture of the empty room. Then a child shows up in full, standing still or not.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: a background image and the recent frames"
#| classes: lc-setup
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. A background image and a list of recent frames for this
# subsection. The background is the median of the clip's frames, as explained further down.
recent_frames = frames
background = np.median(np.array(frames), axis=0).astype(np.uint8)
```

```{python}
foreground = (np.abs(gray.astype(np.int16) - background.astype(np.int16)) > tau).astype(np.uint8)
```

Everything rests on having a good background image, and there are several ways to get one. The simplest is to photograph the empty scene. This is what makes background subtraction fragile, since any change in lighting makes the old snapshot wrong. The KidsRoom handled this by design. Its lighting was held constant whenever the tracker was running and changed only during transitions between story worlds, when vision was switched off ([Bobick et al. 1999, Section 2.3](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/kidsroom.pdf)).

When the scene does change slowly, we can let the background follow it with a *running average*,

$$
B_t = (1 - \alpha)\,B_{t-1} + \alpha\, I_t, \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1 .
$$

Freeman and colleagues subtracted exactly such a running temporal average to remove stationary objects in one of their trackers ([Freeman et al. 1998, Section 5](https://merl.com/publications/docs/TR99-02.pdf)). It is worth unrolling the recursion to see what it really computes. Substituting the formula into itself again and again gives

$$
B_t = \alpha I_t + \alpha(1-\alpha) I_{t-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 I_{t-2} + \cdots = \alpha\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} (1-\alpha)^j I_{t-j}.
$$

This is a weighted average of all past frames in which the weights fall off geometrically, and they sum to α/(1 − (1 − α)) = 1 as an average should. The average age of a frame in this memory is Σ j α(1 − α)^j = (1 − α)/α, so with α = 0.05 the background remembers roughly the last 20 frames. A larger α adapts faster to lighting changes but also absorbs people who stand still for a while, who then fade into the background and vanish.

The running average has a subtler failure, which our test exposed nicely. We started the average from the first frame, which already contained the moving square, and kept updating it as the square moved. At the end the background held a faint *ghost* of the square at its starting position and a smeared trail along its path. Thresholding against this background flagged 2,632 pixels as foreground when the square has only 900. A sturdier choice is the *median* of a stack of frames. As long as each pixel shows background in more than half of the frames, the median ignores the passing object completely. On the same test, the median of our 30 frames gave exactly 900 foreground pixels.

```{python}
stack = np.array(recent_frames)              # shape (number_of_frames, height, width)
background = np.median(stack, axis=0)        # pixel-by-pixel median over time
```

::: {#ex-1-4-3 .exercise}
[**Exercise 1.4.3 (The running average, unrolled)**]{.theorem-title} Write `running_average(frames, alpha)`, which applies B~t~ = (1 − α)B~t−1~ + αI~t~ to a list of frames, starting from B₀ = I₀ and returning the final background as a float array. For a finite list, the unrolled formula of @sec-subtracting-the-background-instead picks up one extra term from the starting frame,

$$
B_t = \sum_{j=0}^{t-1} \alpha(1-\alpha)^j I_{t-j} + (1-\alpha)^t I_0 .
$$

Prove this by induction on t. Then write `unrolled_average(frames, alpha)`, which evaluates the sum directly, with no recursion. The check confirms that the two agree, and then counts the foreground pixels in the last frame against the running average and against the median background, as in our test of @sec-subtracting-the-background-instead.

:::

    """Background after B_t = (1 - alpha) B_{t-1} + alpha I_t over all frames, with B_0 = I_0."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError

def unrolled_average(frames, alpha):

```{python}
#| classes: lc-check
def test():
    alpha = 0.05
    B_rec, B_sum = running_average(frames, alpha), unrolled_average(frames, alpha)
    agree = np.allclose(B_rec, B_sum)
    print("recursion and unrolled sum agree:", agree)
    last = frames[-1].astype(float)
    median_bg = np.median(np.array(frames), axis=0)
    print("foreground pixels against the running average:", int(np.sum(np.abs(last - B_rec) > 30)))
    print("foreground pixels against the median:         ", int(np.sum(np.abs(last - median_bg) > 30)))
    print("the square itself has 900 pixels")
    return agree

check("Exercise 1.4.3", test)
```

### From pixels to blobs {#sec-from-pixels-to-blobs}

A foreground mask is a binary image, and @sec-binary told us how to measure the shape in a binary image. But that only works when there is one object. With four children in the room, we must first decide which foreground pixels belong together. This is the job of *connected component labelling*, covered in the January 25 lecture ([Betke, Jan 25 2024, slides 17 to 29](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-cs585-projections-localization-floodfill-Jan25.pdf)).

First we need to say what "together" means. Two pixels are *4-neighbours* if they share an edge, so each pixel has four of them, above, below, left and right. They are *8-neighbours* if they share an edge or a corner, which adds the four diagonals. A set of foreground pixels is *connected* if we can walk from any of them to any other by steps between neighbours. Neither choice is perfect. If we use 4-neighbours for the objects, a diagonal line of pixels falls apart into single dots. If we use 8-neighbours for both objects and background, a closed ring of diagonal pixels both encloses its inside and lets the inside leak out between the corners. The usual compromise is to use one kind for the objects and the other for the background. Horn devotes much of his Chapter 4 to this surprisingly delicate point.

The slides' first algorithm is *flood fill*. Scan the image row by row until we find a foreground pixel that has no label yet. Give it a new label, then give the same label to all its unlabelled foreground neighbours, and to theirs, and so on until the region is exhausted. Then continue the scan. The slides describe the spreading step recursively, and their critique on slide 25 is that the recursion can build enormous stacks. This is not a theoretical worry. Python refuses to recurse more than about a thousand levels deep, and when we ran the recursive version on a filled 200 × 200 square it crashed with a `RecursionError`. The fix is to keep our own list of pixels still to visit, which can grow as large as memory allows.

```{python}
NEIGHBOURS_4 = [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]

def flood_fill(B, labels, r0, c0, label):
    """Give `label` to every foreground pixel connected to (r0, c0)."""
    h, w = B.shape
    to_visit = [(r0, c0)]               # our own stack, instead of recursion
    labels[r0, c0] = label
    while to_visit:
        r, c = to_visit.pop()
        for dr, dc in NEIGHBOURS_4:
            rr, cc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= rr < h and 0 <= cc < w and B[rr, cc] == 1 and labels[rr, cc] == 0:
                labels[rr, cc] = label
                to_visit.append((rr, cc))

def label_blobs(B):
    labels = np.zeros(B.shape, dtype=int)
    next_label = 1
    for r in range(B.shape[0]):
        for c in range(B.shape[1]):
            if B[r, c] == 1 and labels[r, c] == 0:
                flood_fill(B, labels, r, c, next_label)
                next_label += 1
    return labels, next_label - 1
```

Notice that each pixel is labelled the moment it is pushed onto the list, not when it is popped. Labelling on the pop instead lets the same pixel be pushed many times, which gives the right answer far more slowly.

The slides' alternative is the *sequential labelling algorithm*, which visits every pixel exactly twice. In the first pass we scan row by row and decide each pixel's label by looking only at neighbours we have already visited. Following Horn's naming, which the slides use, call the current pixel A, the pixel to its left B, the pixel above it C and the pixel diagonally above-left D. If none of B, C, D is labelled, A starts a new label. If only D is labelled, A copies it. If one of B or C is labelled, A copies that one. The interesting case is when B and C are both labelled with *different* labels. That happens at the bottom of a U shape, where two arms that looked like separate objects turn out to be joined. We give A either label and write down that the two labels are equivalent. In the second pass, every label is replaced by a single representative of its equivalence class ([Betke, Jan 25 2024, slides 26 to 29](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-cs585-projections-localization-floodfill-Jan25.pdf)).

```{python}
def find(parent, x):
    """Follow the chain of equivalences to the representative label."""
    while parent[x] != x:
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def sequential_label(B):
    h, w = B.shape
    L = np.zeros((h, w), dtype=int)
    parent = {}                                    # label -> an equivalent smaller label
    next_label = 1
    for r in range(h):                             # ---- first pass ----
        for c in range(w):
            if B[r, c] == 0:
                continue
            left = L[r, c - 1] if c > 0 else 0                  # B in Horn's naming
            up = L[r - 1, c] if r > 0 else 0                    # C
            diag = L[r - 1, c - 1] if r > 0 and c > 0 else 0    # D
            if left == 0 and up == 0 and diag == 0:
                L[r, c] = next_label
                parent[next_label] = next_label
                next_label += 1
            elif left == 0 and up == 0:
                L[r, c] = diag
            elif left != 0 and up != 0:
                L[r, c] = left
                a, b = find(parent, left), find(parent, up)
                if a != b:
                    parent[max(a, b)] = min(a, b)      # record the equivalence
            else:
                L[r, c] = left if left != 0 else up
    final = {}                                     # ---- second pass ----
    for lab in parent:
        root = find(parent, lab)
        final.setdefault(root, len(final) + 1)
    for r in range(h):
        for c in range(w):
            if L[r, c] != 0:
                L[r, c] = final[find(parent, L[r, c])]
    return L, len(final)
```

Because it looks at the left, upper and upper-left neighbours, this version joins pixels across one diagonal but not the other. That is called 6-connectivity, and it is Horn's way around the paradox above. We checked the function against SciPy's labelling with the matching six-neighbour pattern on 300 random images and it agreed every time. In practice we use OpenCV's `cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats`, which also measures each blob for us. Real foreground masks are speckled with noise, so we throw away blobs that are too small to be a person.

```{python}
n, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(foreground, connectivity=8)
for i in range(1, n):                         # label 0 is the background
    if stats[i, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA] < 200:      # too small to be a child
        continue
    blob = (labels == i).astype(np.uint8)
    # ... measure area, centroid, orientation and roundness exactly as in Section 1.2 ...
```

```{python}
#| classes: lc-check
def test():
    pic = np.zeros((120, 160), np.uint8)
    cv2.circle(pic, (50, 40), 20, 1, -1)
    pic[95:101, 20:120] = 1
    for r, c in [(10, 150), (60, 100), (110, 5), (70, 140)]:
        pic[r, c] = 1
    table = blob_table(pic, 10)
    for blob in table:
        cx, cy = blob["centroid"]
        print(f"label {blob['label']}: area {blob['area']}, centroid ({cx:.1f}, {cy:.1f}), roundness {blob['roundness']:.3f}")
    diagonal = np.eye(6, dtype=np.uint8)
    print("a diagonal line of 6 pixels has", cv2.connectedComponents(diagonal, connectivity=4)[0] - 1,
          "components with 4-neighbours and", cv2.connectedComponents(diagonal, connectivity=8)[0] - 1, "with 8-neighbours")
    if len(table) != 2:
        return False
    disc, bar = sorted(table, key=lambda blob: -blob["roundness"])
    return (disc["roundness"] > 0.95 and bar["roundness"] < 0.01 and bar["area"] == 600
            and abs(disc["centroid"][0] - 50) < 0.5 and abs(disc["centroid"][1] - 40) < 0.5)

check("Exercise 1.4.4", test)
```

### Motion energy {#sec-motion-energy}

A single difference image is a snapshot of where things changed between two moments. Many movements, like a flap of the arms or a spin, are only recognizable over a longer stretch of time. The KidsRoom slides aggregate T difference images into one binary *motion energy image* by taking their union ([Lecture notes 3, slides 15 and 16](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-kids-room.pdf)),

$$
B_{\text{energy}}(x,y,t) = \bigcup_{i=0}^{T} D(x,y,t-i),
$$

where D(x, y, t) is 1 if pixel (x, y) changed at time t and 0 otherwise. The union is 1 wherever *any* of the recent frames showed a change. The result is a silhouette of the whole region swept out by the movement, and the slides recommend T > 20 frames so that the shape is clearly visible. The idea comes from the work of Davis and Bobick on recognizing human movement, where the same union is taken over the last τ frames and called the motion-energy image ([Bobick and Davis 2001, Section 3.1](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs591/papers/bobick-davis.pdf)).

In code we keep the last T masks and combine them with a logical OR.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: two consecutive frames"
#| classes: lc-setup
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. Two consecutive frames again (the cell in 1.4.2 set prev = cur).
cur = frames[10].astype(np.int16)
prev = frames[9].astype(np.int16)
```

```{python}
from collections import deque

T = 20
recent = deque(maxlen=T)          # a list that forgets its oldest entry automatically

# inside the video loop:
moving = np.abs(cur - prev) > tau
recent.append(moving)
motion_energy = np.any(np.array(recent), axis=0).astype(np.uint8)
```

There is a statistical catch, and it is easy to quantify. Suppose noise alone flags a still pixel with some small probability p in each frame. The union flags it if *any* of T frames does, so the probability becomes

$$
P(\text{false alarm in } B_{\text{energy}}) = 1 - (1-p)^T \approx Tp \quad \text{when } Tp \ll 1 .
$$

The union multiplies the false alarm rate by about T. Our threshold of τ = 15 gives p of a few times 10⁻⁴, which looked negligible frame by frame. Over 20 frames it scattered 66 stray pixels across the still parts of our test video, where a single difference image had shown almost none. So when we take unions over long windows we should raise τ, or remove small blobs afterwards, or both.

Davis and Bobick also defined a richer cousin, the *motion-history image*. Instead of a plain 1, each moving pixel is set to T, and every frame in which it does not move it loses 1, down to zero. Recent motion is bright and older motion fades, so the image records not just where the movement went but in which order. It has a lovely property. It can be updated from the previous history image and the current difference alone, with no stored frames at all. The motion-energy image is recovered by asking where the history is above zero.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: start the motion-history image"
#| classes: lc-setup
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. Start the motion-history image at zero.
mhi = np.zeros(gray.shape)
```

```{python}
# inside the video loop, with mhi = np.zeros(gray.shape) before it starts:
mhi = np.where(moving, T, np.maximum(mhi - 1, 0))
motion_energy = (mhi > 0).astype(np.uint8)
```

Sometimes we do not need a picture of the motion at all, just a number saying how much is going on. Summing the absolute difference over a region gives such a number, and the KidsRoom calls it *energy*.

```{python}
energy = np.sum(np.abs(cur - prev))          # large when there is lots of movement
```

Freeman and colleagues used both versions in their games. A player's arm movements steered a flying character, and the input to the steering was the motion energy image, the absolute difference between successive frames. They computed its moments exactly as in @sec-binary, so that the centre of mass of the motion told the character where to go ([Freeman et al. 1998, Section 2](https://merl.com/publications/docs/TR99-02.pdf)).

#| classes: lc-check
def test():
    mei, mhi_final = motion_images(frames, 20, 15)
    same = np.array_equal(mei.astype(bool), mhi_final > 0)
    print("motion-energy image equals (motion history > 0):", same)
    rows, cols = np.nonzero(mei)
    print(f"centre of mass of the motion energy: x = {cols.mean():.1f}, y = {rows.mean():.1f}")
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5))
    axes[0].imshow(mei, cmap="gray"); axes[0].set_title("motion-energy image")

### The KidsRoom {#sec-the-kidsroom}

We can now read Lecture notes 3 as what it really is, a tour of a working system built almost entirely from the tools in these notes. The KidsRoom, built at the MIT Media Lab and described by Bobick and colleagues in *Presence* in 1999 ([Bobick et al. 1999](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/kidsroom.pdf)), was a mock children's bedroom about 24 by 18 feet, with real furniture, two walls of projected video, and cameras hung from a grid in the ceiling ([Lecture notes 3, slides 5 and 6](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-kids-room.pdf)). Up to four children walked through a story in four worlds. The bedroom came alive, the room became a forest, the bed became a boat on a river, and finally the children danced with monsters.

**Tracking.** An overhead camera, chosen because people rarely hide one another when seen from above, tracked up to four children and the bed as background-difference blobs (slide 13). The paper adds some practical detail. Children entered and left through a known "door" region, so the system could keep count. When two children's blobs merged, the tracker relied on clues like each child's colour and speed to tell them apart again afterwards.

**Rowing.** In the river world the children sit on the bed and row. The slides draw an ellipse that gives the bed's position and orientation (slide 20), and this is exactly the equivalent ellipse of @sec-round-or-elongated, computed from the moments of the bed's blob. The paper explains that the system summed the frame differences separately over each side of the bed to get a rowing energy per side, scaled by the number of people in the boat. Deciding which side a moving pixel is on is a lovely reuse of @sec-orientation. The quantity r = x′ sin θ − y′ cos θ is the signed distance from the bed's long axis, so its sign tells us the side.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: a synthetic bed with movement on one side"
#| classes: lc-setup
# [Setup] Not part of the lecture notes. A synthetic bed tilted by 20 degrees, its centroid and
# orientation computed as in Section 1.2, and a patch of movement on one side of it.
bed = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
cv2.ellipse(bed, (100, 100), (70, 30), 20, 0, 360, 1, -1)
rows, cols = np.nonzero(bed)
x, y = cols.astype(float), rows.astype(float)
x_bar, y_bar = x.mean(), y.mean()
xp, yp = x - x_bar, y - y_bar
a, b, c = np.sum(xp * xp), 2 * np.sum(xp * yp), np.sum(yp * yp)
theta = 0.5 * np.arctan2(b, a - c)
diff = np.zeros((200, 200))
_ = cv2.circle(diff, (90, 75), 8, 50, -1)       # draws in place
```

```{python}
# x_bar, y_bar, theta: the bed's centroid and orientation, from Section 1.2
# diff: absolute frame difference, bed: binary mask of the bed region
ys, xs = np.mgrid[0:diff.shape[0], 0:diff.shape[1]]
r = (xs - x_bar) * np.sin(theta) - (ys - y_bar) * np.cos(theta)   # signed distance to the axis

energy_one_side = np.sum(diff[(r > 0) & (bed == 1)])
energy_other_side = np.sum(diff[(r < 0) & (bed == 1)])
```

We tested this on a synthetic bed tilted at 20° with movement on one side only. The code recovered θ = 20.06° and put all of the energy on the correct side.

**Dancing.** In the monster world, one child stands on each of two rugs and the monsters ask for four dance moves, and each move is recognized in a different way (slides 17 to 19). For the crouch, the slides measure the size of the background-difference blob. The paper adds that an ellipse is fitted to the child's blob and a crouch shows up as a clear drop in its elongation, which is the roundness measure of @sec-round-or-elongated in action. For the Y pose, with arms raised in a Y, the system computed moment-based shape features of the silhouette and compared them with stored examples. The flap and spin moves were recognized by matching temporal templates, which is to say the motion-energy and motion-history images of @sec-motion-energy, again described by their moments.

**What the room teaches.** The last slide draws lessons that apply far beyond children's games (slide 21). The first is that context matters. Recognizing a group of people rowing a boat in an arbitrary video is very hard. Recognizing that the children on the bed are rowing, when the story has just told them to row, is easy, because the story has already ruled out almost everything else. The designers controlled context as well as using it. The monsters tell the children to stay on their own rugs so that the cameras get a clear view. The second lesson is that a story makes people cooperate, which made the vision problem easier still. The third is that algorithms should fail gracefully. When a dance move was recognized with low confidence, the monster on the screen simply did the move without praising the child, so a mistake never broke the spell ([Bobick et al. 1999, Section 3.1](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/kidsroom.pdf)).

It is a fitting place to end. The KidsRoom ran in the late 1990s on six computers far weaker than a phone, with no machine learning to speak of. What it had was frame differences, background subtraction, connected blobs, a few moments and a story clever enough to ask only questions those tools could answer.

::: {#ex-1-4-6 .exercise}
[**Exercise 1.4.6 (Who is rowing harder?)**]{.theorem-title} The starter cell makes a short synthetic river scene, a bed tilted by 20° with two children paddling on it, one on each side of its long axis. Write `rowing_energy(frames, bed)`. It should find the bed's centroid and orientation from the mask `bed`, as in @sec-binary, and return two lists holding the rowing energy on each side of the bed for every pair of consecutive frames, with the side where r > 0 first. The check plots both lists and says which side rowed harder. Is that the child drawn above the bed's axis or the one below it, and does the sign of r agree with what you expected?

:::

```{python}
#| classes: lc-exercise
# [Exercise setup] A synthetic river scene (no need to change these lines).
river_bed = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
cv2.ellipse(river_bed, (100, 100), (70, 30), 20, 0, 360, 1, -1)
_t20 = np.radians(20)
_along, _normal = np.array([np.cos(_t20), np.sin(_t20)]), np.array([np.sin(_t20), -np.cos(_t20)])
river_frames = []
for t in range(40):
    f = np.where(river_bed == 1, 170, 90).astype(float)
    for side, amplitude in [(+1, 12), (-1, 3)]:          # two children, one paddling much harder
        centre = np.array([100.0, 100.0]) + side * 15 * _normal + amplitude * np.sin(t / 2) * _along
        cv2.circle(f, (int(round(centre[0])), int(round(centre[1]))), 6, 40, -1)
    river_frames.append(f.astype(np.uint8))

def rowing_energy(frames, bed):
    """Two lists of per-frame rowing energy, (side where r > 0, side where r < 0)."""
    # your code here
    raise NotImplementedError
```

```{python}
#| classes: lc-check
def test():
    positive, negative = rowing_energy(river_frames, river_bed)
    plt.plot(positive, label="side where r > 0")
    plt.plot(negative, label="side where r < 0")
    plt.xlabel("frame"); plt.ylabel("rowing energy"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
    harder = "r > 0" if sum(positive) > sum(negative) else "r < 0"
    print(f"total energy {sum(positive):.0f} versus {sum(negative):.0f}, so the side where {harder} rowed harder")
    return len(positive) == len(negative) == len(river_frames) - 1 and sum(positive) > 2 * sum(negative)

check("Exercise 1.4.6", test)
```
